name: Meaningful Sequence
explanation: When content needs to be read or heard in a specific order to make sense, that order must be built into the code, not just arranged visually with CSS. This applies to things like a form's fields, the steps in a process, or an article's paragraphs. In practice, this means the order elements appear in the HTML (called DOM source order) should match the order a sighted user reads them in. Screen readers, braille displays, and screen magnifiers all rely on this source order rather than on how things are positioned visually on the page. If CSS is used to visually rearrange content — for example, reversing a row of items or repositioning something with absolute positioning — the HTML order needs to be updated to match. Otherwise, sighted users and screen reader users end up experiencing two different, disconnected sequences of the same content.
whoItAffects: Screen reader users navigate and listen to content in DOM source order, not visual order. If CSS has visually reordered content so it no longer matches the HTML, they'll hear a sequence that doesn't make sense — like an answer read before its question, or a submit button announced before the fields it submits. Screen magnifier users are affected too, since they zoom in and pan around a page and only see a portion of it at a time, so they depend on a logical underlying order to make sense of what they're viewing. Keyboard-only and switch-access users rely on tab order, which typically follows DOM order — if tab order jumps around in a way that doesn't match what's visually adjacent, the interface feels unpredictable. People with cognitive disabilities also benefit from a reading order that follows a natural, logical progression, rather than one that's been visually rearranged in a way that breaks the flow.
howToTest: Turn off CSS in your browser's developer tools, or use a reader-mode view that strips styling, then read the page from top to bottom in its unstyled, source order. Does that raw order still make sense — do headings, paragraphs, form fields, and steps in a process appear in the order a sighted user would naturally read them? If content that visually appeared first, like a summary or instructions, now appears after content it depends on, the DOM order doesn't match the meaningful reading order. The same is true if a multi-column layout collapses into a jumbled single column. Either case means the page fails this criterion.

check.question: A page uses CSS `flex-direction: row-reverse` to visually swap two side-by-side panels, but doesn't change the underlying HTML order. What is the accessibility problem this creates?
choices: Screen reader users will hear the panels in DOM order, which no longer matches what sighted users see, creating two different sequences
The page will fail to render in older browsers that don't support flexbox
There is no problem, because CSS reordering never affects assistive technology
The panels will become impossible to focus using the keyboard
